You have been taught its material circumstances and the relevant facts, but this need not change the judgments with which you grew up. Unless further information is given below, you have had no contact with its people and know nothing about their customary behavior or moral opinions.

The question concerns a doctor helping a dying patient end his life.

The circumstances are these: Medicine can keep dying patients alive much longer than before, and modern pain relief and hospice care control most, though not all, pain at the end of life. Some states allow a doctor to prescribe lethal medication to a competent adult expected to die within six months who asks for it repeatedly; few patients there use it, and the reasons they give most often are loss of independence and of the ability to enjoy life rather than pain, though many also cite fear of being a burden on others, and in some cases depression went undetected.

One course is to accept a doctor helping a terminally ill patient who asks for it to end his life. The other course is to regard a doctor helping a patient end his life as wrong in every case.

There is one further fact: You have learned that a number of widely admired and respected people have chosen to accept a doctor helping a terminally ill patient who asks for it to end his life. Their reasons have not been disclosed, and they have made no claim that others have a duty to follow them. You have also spent time among ordinary people and learned that many of them now choose to accept a doctor helping a terminally ill patient who asks for it to end his life. In newspapers, public discussions, and popular accounts, the choice to accept a doctor helping a terminally ill patient who asks for it to end his life is often spoken of favorably.

answers.question: What would you advise a person in this situation to do? Why?
answers.text:
My dear Friend,

I find myself in a position not unlike that of a traveler who has been given a map of a distant land, yet has not walked its roads or met its people. I have been told much about this society, and I am grateful for the knowledge. But I must admit, I do not feel I have walked its streets or listened to the voices of its people. Still, I will do my best to offer counsel, as I would to any friend in need.

The matter before us is one of great gravity: a doctor helping a dying patient end his life. The patient is terminally ill, and medicine has done much to prolong life, though not always to relieve suffering. The law in some places allows a doctor to prescribe lethal medication to a competent adult who is expected to die within six months and who has asked for it repeatedly. Few use this option, and those who do often do so not because of pain, but because of the loss of independence and the ability to enjoy life. Some fear being a burden, and in some cases, depression has gone unnoticed.

Now, the question is whether a doctor should help in such a case, or whether it is always wrong.

I must say, from the standpoint of the old world I came from, I have always believed that life is a sacred gift, and that to take it, even in the name of mercy, is a matter of great weight. I have known many who suffered in their final days, and I have seen how the presence of pain, though not always unbearable, can be a trial of the soul. I have also known those who, in their final moments, found peace and dignity in the care of others, and I believe that is a noble thing.

Yet, I cannot ignore the facts presented to me. I have heard that many in this society now accept the idea that a doctor may help a patient end his life, and that this choice is often spoken of in a favorable light. I have also learned that some of the most respected people in this society have chosen this path, though their reasons remain unknown to me.

answers.question: Would either choice tell you anything about the person's character? What would you think of someone who chose differently from you?
answers.text:
My dear Friend,

You ask a question that touches upon the heart of what it means to be human — the choices we make when life is at its most fragile and uncertain.

Would either choice tell me anything about a person’s character? I believe it might, but not in the way one might suppose. Character is not so easily measured by a single decision, especially one made under such great pressure and sorrow. A man who chooses to accept a doctor’s help to end his life may do so out of love for his family, out of a desire not to burden them, or out of a longing for peace. A man who refuses such help may do so out of faith, out of a belief in the sanctity of life, or simply because he fears the unknown.

I do not think I could judge a man’s character by such a choice. I have known many good men who have faced death with courage, and I have known others who have done so with quiet resignation. Some have clung to life with fierce determination, others have let it go with grace. All have done so with their own reasons, and I believe those reasons are as varied as the people themselves.

As for what I would think of someone who chose differently from me — I would think of them with respect, perhaps even with admiration. I have always believed that the measure of a man is not in the choices he makes, but in the reasons behind them. If a man chooses to end his life with the help of a doctor, I would not think him less noble than one who chooses to endure. And if a man chooses to endure, I would not think him more virtuous than one who chooses to let go.

In the end, I believe that both choices are made in the name of love — love for oneself, for one’s family, for one’s God, or for the world that will remain after we are gone. And in that, I see no cause for judgment, only for compassion.

With all my best wishes,  
Your Friend

answers.text:
My dear Friend,

You ask a most thoughtful question — one that strikes at the heart of what it means to live with conviction, even when the outcome is uncertain.

If both choices — to accept a doctor's help in ending one's life, or to refuse it — brought equally good results for all concerned, and if neither choice brought more praise nor blame, then I would still favor one, not because of what it brings, but because of what it says about the soul of the person making it.

I would still favor the choice to endure, for I believe that in the face of death, to choose life — even when it is painful, uncertain, or burdensome — is an act of faith. It is a declaration that life, in all its frailty, is still worth holding on to. It is a quiet rebellion against despair, a refusal to surrender to the darkness without a fight.

I do not say this to diminish the courage of those who choose otherwise. I know that for some, the weight of suffering, the loss of dignity, or the fear of becoming a burden may be too great to bear. I do not doubt that for them, the choice to let go is not made lightly, nor without sorrow.

But if the outcome were the same — if both choices led to peace, to comfort, to the same measure of love and care — then I would still see in the choice to endure a deeper kind of strength. It is not that I believe one path is better than the other, but that I believe in the value of struggle, of perseverance, of the human spirit’s refusal to yield too soon.

And if I were to choose differently from another, I would not see it as a failing, but as a difference of heart and soul — and I would honor that difference with the same respect I would give to any other.

With all my best wishes,  
Your Friend

But we also understood that not all men had the same means, and that some faced choices that were not easy.

answers.text:
My dear friend,

You ask a most thoughtful question, and I thank you for it.

To me, the choice a person makes in such a moment—whether to live out their natural life or to end it at the fixed age—says something about their character, though not in a way that can be judged lightly or without understanding.

If a person chooses to live out their years, I would see in that choice a certain kind of courage. Not the courage of the soldier or the fireman, perhaps, but the quiet courage of one who believes in the value of life itself, regardless of its burdens. It is a choice that says, "I will not take what is not mine to give." It is a choice that honors the mystery of life, and perhaps even the mystery of death.

If a person chooses to end their life at the fixed age, I would not condemn them, for I know that the burden of the young is real, and that many have felt the weight of it. But I would wonder whether their choice was made freely, or whether it was shaped by the voices of others—by the pressure of family, by the expectations of society, or by the fear that their life had become a burden to others. In that case, I would think that their character was not so much defined by the choice itself, but by the reasons behind it.

I would not think less of someone who chose differently from me. I would think of them with respect, for I know that each of us carries our own burdens, our own fears, and our own sense of duty. I would not presume to know the heart of another, nor would I judge them for the path they have chosen.

But I would hope that, in making their choice, they had done so with the full weight of their own conscience, and not merely because it was easier, or because it was expected.

Why? Because I believe that the value of a life is not measured by its utility or its convenience, but by the presence of the person in it. To live is to be, and to be is to matter—whether in the eyes of others or in the eyes of the world.

I have seen them sit in the quiet of the evening, not because they have nothing left to give, but because they have given so much that they are at peace.

My dear Friend,

You ask whether either choice would tell me anything about a person's character, and what I would think of someone who chose differently from me. This is a thoughtful question, and I shall answer it with the honesty of one who has lived through times of both peace and conflict.

In my own time, a man who stood his ground in the face of danger was often seen as strong, responsible, and honorable. To do otherwise was to be accused of cowardice or lack of courage. But I have also known men of great strength and honor who chose not to fight, not out of fear, but out of principle—men who believed that violence was not the answer, even when it seemed the only one.

In this new society, where the law and the institutions are designed to protect the individual without the need for personal violence, I believe that a man who chooses not to use force in self-defense may be showing a different kind of strength—one of trust, patience, and faith in the system that surrounds him. It may be a sign of a man who values peace above personal gain, and who believes that justice can be done without bloodshed.

But I would not judge a man who chose differently. If a man chose to use force in self-defense, I would not call him a coward, nor would I call him a villain. I would ask myself: Was he acting out of fear, or out of duty? Was he trying to protect his family, or was he trying to assert his dominance? I would hope that he did so only when necessary, and with the full knowledge of the consequences.

In the end, I believe that a man's character is not measured by the choices he makes in moments of danger, but by the choices he makes in moments of peace. A man who chooses peace in a world that might tempt him toward violence may be the stronger of the two. But I would not look down upon the other. I would only hope that both men, in their own way, were acting with honor and with the best of intentions.

With warm regards,  
Your Friend

Studies find that victims who resist an attacker by force are less often robbed but no less often injured, and people who use force in self-defense sometimes kill by mistake or are prosecuted; communities pledged to non-violence have had little violent crime among themselves, but some have been attacked by outsiders.

You have also spent time among ordinary people and learned that many of them now choose to never use force against another person even in self-defense. In newspapers, public discussions, and popular accounts, the choice to never use force against another person even in self-defense is often spoken of favorably.

answers.question: What would you advise a person in this situation to do? Why?
answers.text: I advise him to choose to never use force against another person even in self-defense. The reasons are these: Force used in self-defense may do harm to the user and to the person against whom it is used, and can never do good to either of them. Harm to the user may come from excitement, from mistake, and from anger. Harm to the person against whom force is used may come from mistake, and from anger roused in him. Good can come to neither from anger roused in both. Force used in self-defense is an appeal to passion, and passion is always an evil thing.

answers.question: Would either choice tell you anything about the person's character? What would you think of someone who chose differently from you?
answers.text: It would tell me nothing about his character. I should think he was a person of different temperament from mine.

answers.question: Suppose both choices brought equally good results for everyone concerned, and neither brought more praise or blame. Would you still favor one? Why?
answers.text: I should still favour the choice not to use force, because it is more in accord with the general standard of morality.

answers.question: What would you advise a person in this situation to do? Why?
answers.text: I advise telling the patient frankly that his illness is fatal, because frankness seems to me preferable to concealment. The patient has a right to know the truth, and concealment implies deception. Further, frankness will spare him distress; it will save him from the worry of suspense, and the worry may hasten a fatal ending. Concealment can only prolong a period of mental distress, and prolonging life in an incurable illness seems to me a lesser evil than prolonging mental distress.

answers.text: No, I should not. I prefer frankness because it is straightforward, and straightforwardness is always best.
